In [[probability theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''white noise analysis''', otherwise known as Hida calculus, is a framework for infinite-dimensional and [[stochastic calculus]], based on the [[Gaussian white noise]] [[probability space]], to be compared with [[Malliavin calculus]] based on the [[Wiener process]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Introduction to Infinite-Dimensional Stochastic Analysis|last1=Huang|first1=Zhi-yuan|last2=Yan|first2=Jia-An|date=2000|publisher=Springer Netherlands|isbn=9789401141086|location=Dordrecht|oclc=851373497}}</ref> It was initiated by Takeyuki Hida in his 1975 Carleton Mathematical Lecture Notes.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Stochastic Systems: Modeling, Identification and Optimization, I|volume = 5|last=Hida|first=Takeyuki|date=1976|publisher=Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-642-00783-5|series=Mathematical Programming Studies|pages=53–59|language=en|doi=10.1007/bfb0120763|chapter = Analysis of Brownian functionals|url = http://purl.umn.edu/4378}}</ref>

The term [[white noise]] was first used for signals with a flat spectrum.

== White noise measure==
The white noise [[probability measure]] <math>\mu</math> on the space <math>S'(\mathbb{R})</math> of [[tempered distributions]] has the [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Hida|first1=Takeyuki|last2=Kuo|first2=Hui-Hsiung|last3=Potthoff|first3=Jürgen|last4=Streit|first4=Ludwig|title=White Noise |language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/978-94-017-3680-0|year = 1993|isbn = 978-90-481-4260-6}}</ref>

: <math>C(f)=\int_{S'(\mathbb{R})}\exp \left( i\left\langle \omega ,f\right\rangle
\right) \, d\mu (\omega )=\exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^2(t) \, dt\right), \quad f\in S(\mathbb{R}). </math>

=== Brownian motion in white noise analysis ===
A version of Wiener's Brownian motion <math>B(t)</math> is obtained by the [[dual pair]]ing

: <math>B(t) = \langle \omega, 1\!\!1_{[0,t)}\rangle, </math>

where <math>1\!\!1_{[0,t)}</math> is the [[indicator function]] of the interval <math>[0,t)
</math>. Informally

: <math>B(t)=\int_0^t \omega(t) \, dt</math>

and in a generalized sense

: <math>\omega(t)=\frac{d B(t)}{dt}.</math>

== Hilbert space ==
Fundamental to white noise analysis is the [[Hilbert space]]

: <math>(L^2):=L^2\left( S'(\mathbb{R}),\mu \right), </math>

generalizing the Hilbert spaces <math>L^2(\mathbb{R}^n,e^{-\frac{1}{2} x^2}d^n x) </math> to infinite dimension.

=== [[Polynomial chaos|Wick polynomials]] ===
An orthonormal basis in this Hilbert space, generalizing that of [[Hermite polynomials]], is given by the so-called "Wick", or "[[normal order]]ed" polynomials <math>\left\langle {:\omega^n:} , f_n\right\rangle </math> with <math>{:\omega^n:} \in S'(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> and <math>f_n \in S(\mathbb{R}^n) </math>

with normalization

: <math>\int_{S'(\mathbb{R})}\left\langle :\omega^n:,f_n \right\rangle^2 \, d\mu(\omega) = n!\int f_{n}^2(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \, d^n x, </math>

entailing the Itô-Segal-Wiener isomorphism of the white noise Hilbert space <math>(L^2) </math> with [[Fock space]]:

: <math>L^2\left( S'(\mathbb{R}),\mu \right) \simeq \bigoplus\limits_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname{Sym} L^2(\mathbb{R}^n,n! \, d^n x). </math>

The "chaos expansion"

: <math>\varphi(\omega) =\sum_n \left\langle :\omega^n:, f_n\right\rangle </math>

in terms of [[Wick ordered|Wick polynomials]] correspond to the expansion in terms of multiple [[Wiener integral]]s. Brownian [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingales]] <math>M_t(\omega) </math> are characterized by kernel functions <math>f_n </math> depending on <math>t </math> only a "cut-off":

: <math>f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t)=
\begin{cases}
f_n (x_1,\ldots,x_n) & \text{if } i x_i\leq t, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>

=== [[Gelfand triple]]s ===
Suitable restrictions of the kernel function <math>\varphi _{n} </math> to be smooth and rapidly decreasing in <math>x </math> and <math>n </math> give rise to spaces of white noise [[Distribution (mathematics)#Definitions of test functions and distributions|test functions]] <math>\varphi </math>, and, by [[Duality (mathematics)|duality]], to spaces of [[generalized function]]s <math>\Psi </math> of white noise, with

: <math id="dual">\left\langle \! \left\langle \Psi ,\varphi \right\rangle \!\right\rangle
:=\sum_n n!\left\langle \psi_n,\varphi_n \right\rangle </math>

generalizing the scalar product in <math>(L^2) </math>. Examples are the Hida triple, with

: <math>\varphi \in (S)\subset (L^2)\subset (S)^\ast \ni \Psi  </math>

or the more general Kondratiev triples.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Kondrat'ev|first1=Yu.G.|last2=Streit|first2=L.|title=Spaces of White Noise distributions: constructions, descriptions, applications. I|journal=Reports on Mathematical Physics|volume=33|issue=3|pages=341–366|doi=10.1016/0034-4877(93)90003-w|year=1993|bibcode=1993RpMP...33..341K }}</ref>

== T- and S-transform ==
Using the white noise test functions

: <math>\varphi_f(\omega ):=\exp \left( i\left\langle \omega ,f\right\rangle \right) \in (S),\quad f \in S(\mathbb{R})  </math>

one introduces the "T-transform" of white noise distributions <math>\Psi </math> by setting

: <math>T\Psi (f):=\left\langle \!\left\langle \Psi ,\varphi _{f}\right\rangle
\!\right\rangle .  </math>

Likewise, using

: <math>\phi_f(\omega ):=\exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}\int f^2(t) \, dt\right) \exp\left( -\left\langle \omega ,f\right\rangle \right) \in (S)  </math>

one defines the "S-transform" of white noise distributions <math>\Psi </math> by

: <math>S\Psi (f):=\left\langle \!\left\langle \Psi ,\phi_f\right\rangle\!
\right\rangle,\quad f \in S(\mathbb{R}).  </math>

It is worth noting that for [[generalized function]]s <math>\Psi</math>, {{clarify|text=with kernels <math>\psi_n </math> as in ,|reason=As in what?|date=May 2018}} the S-transform is just

: <math>S\Psi (f)=\sum n!\left\langle \psi_n,f^{\otimes n}\right\rangle.  </math>

Depending on the choice of Gelfand triple, the white noise test functions and distributions are characterized by corresponding growth and analyticity properties of their S- or T-transforms.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

=== Characterization theorem===
<blockquote>The function <math>G(f) </math> is the T-transform of a (unique) Hida distribution <math>\Psi </math> iff for all <math>f_1,f_2\in S(R), </math> the function <math>z\mapsto G(zf_1+f_2) </math> is analytic in the whole complex plane and of second order exponential growth, i.e. <math display="block">\left\vert G(\ f)\right\vert <ae^{bK(f,f)}, </math>where <math>K </math> is some continuous quadratic form on <math>S'(\mathbb{R})\times S'(\mathbb{R})</math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kuo|first1=H.-H.|last2=Potthoff|first2=J.|last3=Streit|first3=L.|date=1991|title=A characterization of white noise test functionals|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.nmj/1118782788|journal=Nagoya Mathematical Journal|language=en|volume=121|pages=185–194|issn=0027-7630|doi=10.1017/S0027763000003469|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kondratiev|first1=Yu.G.|last2=Leukert|first2=P.|last3=Potthoff|first3=J.|last4=Streit|first4=L.|last5=Westerkamp|first5=W.|title=Generalized Functionals in Gaussian Spaces: The Characterization Theorem Revisited|journal=Journal of Functional Analysis|volume=141|issue=2|pages=301–318|doi=10.1006/jfan.1996.0130|year=1996|arxiv=math/0303054|s2cid=58889052}}</ref></blockquote>The same is true for S-transforms, and similar characterization theorems hold for the more general [[Yuri Kondratiev|Kondratiev]] distributions.<ref name=":1" />

== Calculus ==
For test functions <math>\varphi \in (S) </math>, partial, directional derivatives exist:

: <math>\partial_\eta \varphi (\omega ):=\lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0}\frac{\varphi (\omega +\varepsilon \eta )-F(\omega )} \varepsilon  </math>

where <math>\omega </math> may be varied by any generalized function <math>\eta </math>. In particular, for the Dirac distribution <math>\eta =\delta _{t} </math> one defines the "Hida derivative", denoting

: <math>\partial_t \varphi (\omega ):=\lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{\varphi(\omega +\varepsilon \delta_t)-F(\omega )} \varepsilon.  </math>

Gaussian [[integration by parts]] yields the dual operator on distribution space

: <math display="block">\partial_t^\ast =-\partial_t+\omega(t) </math>

An infinite-dimensional gradient

: <math>\nabla :(S)\rightarrow L^2(R,dt) \otimes (S) </math>

is given by

: <math>\nabla F(t,\omega) =\partial_t F(\omega). </math>

The Laplacian <math>\triangle </math> ("[[Laplace–Beltrami operator]]") with

: <math>-\triangle =\int dt\;\partial_t^\ast \partial_t \geq 0  </math>

plays an important role in infinite-dimensional analysis and is the image of the [[Fock space]] number operator.

== Stochastic integrals ==
A stochastic integral, the [[Hitsuda–Skorokhod integral]], can be defined for suitable families <math>\Psi (t) </math> of white noise distributions as a [[Pettis integral]]

: <math>\int \partial_t^\ast \Psi (t) \, dt\in (S)^\ast, </math>

generalizing the [[Itô integral]] beyond adapted integrands.

== Applications ==
In general terms, there are two features of white noise analysis that have been prominent in applications.<ref>{{Cite book|title=White noise analysis and quantum information|editor-last=Accardi |editor-first=Luigi |isbn=9789813225459 |location=Singapore |publisher=World Scientific Publishing |oclc=1007244903|last1 = Accardi|first1 = Luigi|last2=Chen|first2=Louis Hsiao Yun|last3=Ohya|first3=Masanori|last4=Hida|first4=Takeyuki|last5=Si|first5=Si|date=June 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Methods and applications of white noise analysis in interdisciplinary sciences |last1=Bernido |first1=Christopher C. |last2=Carpio-Bernido |first2=M. Victoria |isbn=9789814569118 |publisher=World Scientific |location=New Jersey|oclc=884440293|year = 2015}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Stochastic partial differential equations : a modeling, white noise functional approach|date=2010|publisher=Springer|first1=Helge |last1=Holden |first2=Bernt |last2=Øksendal |last3=Ubøe |first3=Jan |author4=Tusheng Zhang |isbn=978-0-387-89488-1|edition= 2nd |location=New York|oclc=663094108}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Let us use white noise|editor1=Hida, Takeyuki |editor2-last=Streit |editor2-first= Ludwig |year=2017 |isbn=9789813220935|location=New Jersey|oclc=971020065 |publisher=World Scientific}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Stochastic Analysis: Classical and Quantum|language=en-US|doi=10.1142/5962|year=2005|editor1-last=Hida|editor1-first=Takeyuki|isbn=978-981-256-526-6}}</ref>

First, white noise is a generalized [[stochastic process]] with independent values at each time.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Generalized functions |volume=4, Applications of harmonic analysis |last1=Gelfand |first1=Izrail Moiseevitch |first2=Naum Âkovlevič |last2=Vilenkin |first3=Amiel |last3=Feinstein|date=1964 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-279504-6|location=New York|oclc=490085153}}</ref> Hence it plays the role of a generalized system of independent coordinates, in the sense that in various contexts it has been fruitful to express more general processes occurring e.g. in engineering or [[mathematical finance]], in terms of white noise.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Biagini|first1=Francesca|author1-link=Francesca Biagini|last2=Øksendal|first2=Bernt|last3=Sulem|first3=Agnès|author3-link=Agnès Sulem|last4=Wallner|first4=Naomi|date=2004-01-08|title=An introduction to white–noise theory and Malliavin calculus for fractional Brownian motion|url=http://rspa.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/460/2041/347|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|language=en|volume=460|issue=2041|pages=347–372|doi=10.1098/rspa.2003.1246|bibcode=2004RSPSA.460..347B |issn=1364-5021|hdl=10852/10633|s2cid=120225816|hdl-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

Second, the [[#Characterization theorem|characterization theorem]] given above allows various heuristic expressions to be identified as generalized functions of white noise. This is particularly effective to attribute a well-defined mathematical meaning to so-called "[[functional integral]]s". [[Feynman integral]]s in particular have been given rigorous meaning for large classes of quantum dynamical models.

Noncommutative extensions of the theory have grown under the name of quantum white noise, and finally, the [[rotational invariance]] of the white noise characteristic function provides a framework for representations of infinite-dimensional rotation groups.
